issues.description: trainer_args key inconsistency: 'max_step' read but docstring says 'max_steps' — one of them is wrong and will KeyError
issues.detail: The docstring lists `max_steps`, `log_interval`, `val_interval`, `save_interval`, `deepspeed_config`. The code reads `trainer_args["max_step"]` (singular). Additionally `val_interval` is documented but never read; `log_interval` is read but never used (logging happens every step). Two facts about the same thing have been complected: the config key, the docstring contract, and the actual behavior. Pick one name, read it, document it, and use it — or this fails on the first real config that follows the docstring.

issues.description: run() loop has no termination on empty iterator and global_step can overshoot max_step silently
issues.detail: `while self.global_step < self.max_step` wraps `train()` which itself loops over `save_interval` steps incrementing global_step. There is no per-step check against max_step inside train(), so the loop will overshoot by up to save_interval-1 steps, and it saves a checkpoint after every train+valid pass regardless of whether progress was made. The time semantics of "stop at max_step" are complected with "save every save_interval" — those are two separate facts and should be checked separately.

issues.description: _all_reduce_stats mutates caller's dict in place and changes value semantics (sum vs mean) — value vs identity confusion
issues.detail: The function takes a dict of tensors, mutates them in place via async all_reduce (SUM), then rebinds `stats[key] = stats[key] / world_size`. The caller's `out["stats"]` is the same object; the model's returned stats now have post-reduction values living inside the model's output structure. This is the textbook value/identity/time complecting: a returned 'value' is being mutated by a reducer that pretends to be pure. Return a new dict of reduced values; leave the input alone.

issues.description: Checkpoint discovery uses string splitting on directory names instead of a manifest file
issues.detail: `sorted(..., key=lambda x: int(x.name.split("step_")[-1]))` treats the filesystem as the source of truth for 'which checkpoint is latest' and encodes the step number in the directory name. A `latest` symlink or a small `checkpoints/manifest.json` listing {step: path} makes the identity (latest checkpoint) explicit and decouples it from the place-oriented name parsing. Right now any stray directory containing 'step_' breaks the sort.

issues.description: wandb is complected into the trainer as a mandatory global side-effect channel
issues.detail: The docstring announces wandb is MANDATORY, the trainer calls `wandb.config.update` and `wandb.log` directly, and rank-1+ processes initialize wandb in 'disabled' mode in train.py just to satisfy the contract. This is easy-not-simple: wandb-as-global is familiar, but it conflates 'a metric was produced' with 'a metric was logged to wandb'. Pass a logger callback (or list of sinks) into the trainer; let the caller wire wandb if they want it. The trainer's job is training, not telemetry transport.

issues.description: freeze_param matching is a prefix-string check on parameter names — incidental complexity from a string protocol
issues.detail: `k.startswith(t + ".") or k == t` defines a half-baked path language on module names. The user has to know that 'encoder' freezes 'encoder.*' but not 'encoder_extra.*'. The actual concern is 'a set of submodules to freeze.' Take a list of module paths, resolve each to a submodule via `model.get_submodule`, iterate its parameters. The data (which modules) is then explicit, and the matching rule disappears.

issues.description: valid() averages floats-of-tensors after all-reduce — double-averaging across rank and across batches with no weighting
issues.detail: Per batch: SUM-then-divide-by-world-size (mean across ranks). Then per dataset: arithmetic mean of those per-batch means. If batches have different sizes (which is common with batchfy_method by length), this is not the true validation mean — it's the mean of batch-means. The 'value' you want (true average loss over all valid samples) is being approximated by an easy-not-simple aggregation. Track (sum, count) tuples and divide once at the end, or weight by batch size.

issues.description: train_dtype derives dtype from ds_config dict shape instead of from the initialized engine
issues.detail: After `deepspeed.initialize`, the engine knows its precision authoritatively. Reading the JSON dict afterward and re-deriving dtype duplicates that fact in two places — one will drift. Ask the engine: `self.model_engine.communication_data_type` or check `self.model_engine.bfloat16_enabled()` / `fp16_enabled()`. One source of truth for 'what dtype is training in.'

issues.description: train.py mixes argparse hyphens and underscores inconsistently, complecting CLI surface with Python attribute names
issues.detail: `--train-config`, `--output-dir`, `--stats-dir` use hyphens (argparse maps to underscores). But `--local_rank` and `--resume_path` use underscores. The CLI is one fact (the user-visible flag names); the attribute names are another. Pick one convention for the CLI. Right now users have to remember which flags take which separator, and that's incidental complexity from the writing process leaking out.

issues.description: valid_iterator_args is built once then passed via **kwargs to many factories, hiding the time of the rank/world_size capture
issues.detail: It's a shared dict mutated nowhere but reused everywhere. That's fine in itself, but the construction-time facts (rank, world_size, stats_dir, collate_fn) are smuggled in as kwargs while `unregistered_specifier` / `registered_specifier` come positionally. Two ways to specify the same factory's inputs makes the factory's contract harder to read. Pass a single dataclass/dict of 'shared loader config' explicitly, and let the per-spec arg be the only variable.

issues.description: specifier strings 'task:name:data_json[:factor]' are an ad-hoc encoding of a data structure
issues.detail: A space-separated list of colon-separated 4-tuples is being parsed at every entry point. The values (task, name, json path, factor) are real data — give them a real shape. A YAML/JSON list of {task, name, json, factor} entries in the train config eliminates the parsing layer entirely and removes the 'is the factor present' ambiguity. The string format is easy (one CLI flag) but not simple (a parser, a docstring, four entry-points to keep in sync).

issues.description: Logging strings used f-string inside logger.info — fine here, but the rank-aware format string is constructed once and frozen
issues.detail: `log_format` interpolates rank/world_size at config-time, not at log-time. That's simple in this case (rank doesn't change), so it's fine. Noting it because if someone later adds dynamic context (job_id, step), they'll be tempted to rebuild basicConfig, which won't work. Consider a logging Filter that injects context per record.

issues.description: `(self.output_dir / "checkpoints").mkdir(exist_ok=True, parents=True)` then later `.exists()` check is redundant
issues.detail: The directory is guaranteed to exist after __init__, so the `elif (self.output_dir / "checkpoints").exists()` branch in _load_checkpoint is always taken when resume_path is None. The list might be empty, which is correctly handled, but the `.exists()` check is dead. Small thing; remove it for clarity.

review.summary: This PR introduces two files that try to be a training launcher and a DeepSpeed trainer. They mostly work, but they have complected several concerns: the trainer-args contract (docstring says `max_steps`, code reads `max_step`), the all-reduce that mutates the model's returned stats dict in place, wandb-as-mandatory-global, an ad-hoc string protocol for data specifiers, and a string-parsing checkpoint discovery scheme. The essential complexity here is real (distributed training, mixed precision, resumable checkpoints), but a meaningful chunk of what's in the diff is incidental — the easy choices (global wandb, string specifiers, prefix-match freeze, mean-of-batch-means) have been mistaken for the simple ones. Two P0 bugs (key name mismatch, run-loop overshoot) need fixing before merge; the rest are decomposition opportunities that will compound as the trainer grows. The question that should have been asked first: what is the single source of truth for training state (step, dtype, latest checkpoint, metrics) — and who reads each of those facts from where.
